entry: Mountain in the Black Hills of South Dakota, carved with colossal sculptures of four U.S. presidents. Sculptor Gutzon Borglum oversaw the carving from 1927 to 1941. The heads, each 60-foot-tall (18 m), depict [[George Washington]], [[Thomas Jefferson]], [[Theodore Roosevelt]] and [[Abraham Lincoln]]. The memorial attracts more than two million visitors annually. The mountain stands on land taken from the [[Sioux|Sioux Nation]] in the 1870s. In 1980 the U.S. Supreme Court ruled that the taking required just compensation and awarded the tribe $102 million, but the Sioux have refused the money and continue to demand return of the land.

Active [[Stratovolcano|stratovolcano]] in Skamania County, Washington, 52 miles (83 km) northeast of [[Portland, Oregon|Portland]], in the [[Pacific Northwest]] region of the United States. The volcano's English name honors the British diplomat Alleyne FitzHerbert, 1st Baron St Helens. Its eruption on May 18, 1980, was the most economically destructive volcanic event in U.S. history. Triggered by a magnitude 5.1 [[Earthquake|earthquake]], a debris avalanche caused a lateral eruption that reduced the summit from 9,677 to 8,363 ft (2,950 to 2,549 m). The eruption killed 57 people and destroyed 200 homes, 47 bridges, 15 miles (24 km) of railways and 185 miles (298 km) of highway. Volcanic activity continued until 2008. In 1982 Congress established the Mount St. Helens National Volcanic Monument.

Sacred mountain in [[Shandong]] province, eastern China, regarded as the foremost of China's Sacred Mountains. It is associated with sunrise, birth and renewal. Located north of the city of Tai'an and south of the provincial capital [[Jinan]], it is the highest point in the province. Its tallest peak, Jade Emperor Peak, rises 1,532.7 meters (5,029 ft) above sea level. Traces of human presence date to the [[Paleolithic]] period. The mountain has been a place of worship for at least 3,000 years and served as one of China's most important ceremonial centers. It was designated a [[UNESCO]] World Heritage Site in 1987 for its sacred importance and dramatic landscape.

Active [[Stratovolcano|stratovolcano]] on the Gulf of Naples in [[Campania]], Italy, about 9 km (5.6 mi) east of [[Naples]]. Its [[Eruption of Mount Vesuvius in 79 AD|eruption in 79 AD]] destroyed the Roman cities of [[Pompeii]], Herculaneum, Oplontis and Stabiae. The eruption ejected a cloud of stones, ash and volcanic gases to a height of 33 km (21 mi). More than 1,000 people are thought to have died, and the only surviving witness account consists of two letters by Pliny the Younger to the historian [[Tacitus]]. Vesuvius has erupted many times since and is the only volcano on Europe's mainland to have erupted in the last hundred years. Marked as one of the Decade Volcanoes, it is regarded as one of the world's most dangerous, because 3,000,000 people live near enough to be affected by an eruption, with at least 600,000 in the danger zone.

Mountain in California's [[Sierra Nevada]], the highest point in the contiguous United States, at 14,505 feet (4,421 m). It lies on the border of Inyo and Tulare counties. The summit is the southern terminus of the [[John Muir|John Muir Trail]], which runs 211.9 mi (341.0 km) from Happy Isles in Yosemite Valley. Mount Whitney is the tallest mountain in the United States outside [[Alaska]].

Navigable route through a [[Mountain range|mountain range]] or over a ridge. Because ranges are formidable barriers to travel, passes have long played a key role in trade, war, and human and animal migration. Passes are typically formed between two volcanic peaks or created by erosion from water, ice or wind. The lowest point along a ridge, the saddle, often provides the route, and the top of a pass is frequently the only flat ground in the area. Roads and railways have long been built through passes, and some high ones have tunnels, such as the Eisenhower Tunnel beneath Loveland Pass in the Rockies. Where a national border follows a ridge, a pass is typically on the border; [[Argentina]] and [[Chile]] share a 5,300 kilometers (3,300 mi) border that includes 42 mountain passes. The Brenner Pass in the [[Alps]] is a typical historic trade route.

Series of mountains or hills arranged in a line and connected by high ground. A mountain system or belt is a group of ranges with similar form, structure and alignment that arose from the same cause, usually an orogeny. Most significant ranges on Earth result from [[Plate tectonics|plate tectonics]]. Ranges are usually segmented by highlands, [[Mountain pass|mountain passes]] and valleys. Most young ranges on the land surface are associated with the [[Ring of Fire|Pacific Ring of Fire]] or the Alpide belt. The [[Andes]], often considered the world's longest mountain system, are 7,000 kilometers (4,350 mi) long. The [[Himalayas]] contain the highest mountains, including [[Mount Everest]], which is 8,848 meters (29,029 ft) high. Air rising over a range cools and drops its moisture, leaving a rain shadow on the leeward side, and erosion gradually wears mountains down into low hills and plains.

Outdoor activity involving the ascent of mountains, including traditional [[Climbing|climbing]], [[Skiing]] and via ferratas. In everyday language the term is synonymous with mountain climbing or alpinism. Unlike most sports, mountaineering lacks widely applied formal rules and governance; practitioners follow a variety of techniques and philosophies, and local alpine clubs provide resources and social activities. The International Climbing and Mountaineering Federation (UIAA) is the world organization for the sport and is recognized by the International Olympic Committee. In 1492 Antoine de Ville climbed Mont Aiguille using ropes, ladders and iron hooks, an ascent widely recognized as the birth of mountaineering. In 1786 Jacques Balmat claimed a reward offered by Horace-Bénédict de Saussure for the first ascent of [[Mont Blanc]].

Small [[Rodent|rodent]] with a pointed snout, small rounded ears and a body-length scaly tail. The best-known species is the [[House mouse|common house mouse]] (*Mus musculus*). Mice are typically distinguished from [[Rat|rats]] by size, although the name is not confined to the genus *Mus*. The white lab mouse, with its more uniform traits, is widely used in research. Cats, [[Dog|wild dogs]], [[Fox|foxes]], birds of prey, snakes and some large lizards prey on mice, yet mouse populations remain plentiful. Mice spread disease through their [[Feces|feces]] and are often carriers of parasites; in North America, breathing dust contaminated with mouse excrement has been linked to hantavirus. As primarily nocturnal animals, mice compensate for poor eyesight with a keen sense of hearing and rely on smell to locate food. In the wild they build intricate burrows with long entrances and escape tunnels.

Growth of facial hair above the upper lip and below the nose, mostly on men. Mustaches have been worn in many styles throughout history. The word is French, derived from Italian, and ultimately from a Greek word meaning "upper lip" or "facial hair." One of the earliest documents of mustaches without beards comes from Iron Age [[Celts]], according to the Greek historian Diodorus Siculus, whose account describes Gallic nobles letting their mustaches grow until they covered the mouth. Mustaches remained common through the [[Middle Ages]], and their popularity in the West peaked in the 1880s and 1890s. In many 20th-century Arab countries, mustaches were associated with power, while [[Beard|beards]] were associated with Islamic traditionalism. In Islam, trimming the mustache is considered a recommended practice. After [[Adolf Hitler]] adopted the narrow toothbrush mustache, it became stigmatized in post-1945 Western fashion.

Body opening through which many animals ingest food and vocalize. The oral cavity behind it is the first part of the alimentary canal, which leads to the pharynx and gullet. In [[Tetrapod|tetrapods]], the mouth is bounded by the lips and cheeks, and the oral cavity, from Latin bucca, meaning "cheek," is also called the buccal cavity. It contains the [[Tongue]]. Except for some groups such as birds and lissamphibians, [[Vertebrate|vertebrates]] usually have teeth, although some fish have pharyngeal teeth instead of oral teeth. Most [[Bilateria|bilaterian]] animals, including arthropods, mollusks and chordates, have a gut tube with a mouth at one end and an [[Anus|anus]] at the other. Which end forms first in [[Ontogeny|ontogeny]] is used to classify bilaterians as protostomes or deuterostomes. Sponges have no mouth or gut and instead capture food by endocytosis.

Venue containing auditoriums for the public viewing of films. Most are commercial operations that sell tickets to audiences. Films are projected onto a large screen at the front of each auditorium, and sound plays through wall-mounted speakers, with subwoofers used for low-pitched sounds since the 1970s. Since the 2010s most theaters have been equipped for digital projection. The largest complexes, called multiplexes, were developed in Canada in the 1950s and can have up to thirty screens. Audiences sit on padded seats, usually set on a sloped floor. Theaters typically sell soft drinks, [[Popcorn|popcorn]] and [[Candy|candy]], and some sell [[Fast food|fast food]]. In some jurisdictions they may be licensed to sell alcoholic drinks. The first commercial film screenings took place in Paris in 1895, presented by the [[Lumière brothers]].

Arm of the [[Indian Ocean]] between [[Madagascar]] and [[Mozambique]] in southeastern Africa. The channel is about 1,700 km (900 nmi; 1,100 mi) long and 419 km (226 nmi; 260 mi) across at its narrowest point. It reaches a depth of 3,292 m (10,801 ft) about 230 km (124 nmi; 143 mi) off the coast of Mozambique. A warm current, the Mozambique Current, flows southward through the channel and leads into the Agulhas Current off the east coast of [[Southern Africa|southern Africa]]. Its warm waters support coral reefs, mangroves and seagrass beds, and its fisheries provide livelihoods for coastal populations in Mozambique, Tanzania and the [[Comoros]]. Offshore areas hold natural gas reserves, which have driven exploration and development.

Country in southeastern Africa on the Indian Ocean, with its capital at [[Maputo]] (pop., 2024: 34,777,605). It borders [[Tanzania]], [[Malawi]], [[Zambia]], [[Zimbabwe]], Eswatini and [[South Africa]], and it is separated from Madagascar by the [[Mozambique Channel]]. Swahili port towns developed on its coast between the 7th and 11th centuries. Portuguese colonization began in 1505, after [[Vasco da Gama]] reached the area in 1498. Mozambique gained independence in 1975, and a civil war lasted from 1977 to 1992. It held its first multiparty elections in 1994 and has since remained a relatively stable presidential republic, although a low-intensity insurgency persists mainly in remote regions. The economy is based chiefly on fishing and agriculture, with growing food, chemical, aluminum and oil industries. Portuguese is the only official language, and Christianity is the most popular religion. Despite rich natural resources, it remains one of the world's poorest and least developed countries.

American YouTuber, entrepreneur and philanthropist known for high-production challenge videos. His main channel is the most subscribed on [[YouTube]]. He founded Beast Industries, a [[Conglomerate (company)|conglomerate]] whose businesses include Feastables and Lunchly. He co-founded Team Trees, a fundraiser that raised more than $24 million for tree planting, and Team Seas, which raised over $30 million for ocean conservation. He also created the reality competition series Beast Games.

British television sitcom (1990–1995) created by [[Rowan Atkinson]] and Richard Curtis, starring Atkinson as the title character. The character was developed while Atkinson studied at the [[University of Oxford]]. The series centers on a man described as "a child in a grown man's body" who solves everyday problems and often causes disruption. Its physical comedy draws on [[Silent film|early silent films]] and the work of Jacques Tati. The episode "The Trouble with Mr. Bean" drew 18.74 million viewers, and the series has been sold in 245 territories. It spawned an animated spin-off and two theatrical films.

Title awarded to the winner of the annual professional men's open-division [[Bodybuilding|bodybuilding]] contest, held as part of the Olympia Fitness & Performance Weekend. Joe Weider created the contest so that amateur Mr. Universe winners could keep competing and earn money. The first was held on September 18, 1965, at the Brooklyn Academy of Music in [[New York City]]. Lee Haney and [[Ronnie Coleman]] each hold the record of eight wins. The film *Pumping Iron* (1977) covered the 1975 contest in [[Pretoria]], South Africa, and helped launch the acting careers of [[Arnold Schwarzenegger]] and [[Lou Ferrigno]].

American actor and retired professional wrestler, born Laurence Tureaud. He grew up in [[Chicago]]'s housing projects and adopted the name Mr. T as a mark of self-respect. He is known for the role of B. A. Baracus in the 1980s series *The A-Team* and for playing the boxer Clubber Lang in *Rocky III* (1982). He is also known for his mohawk haircut, gold jewelry and catchphrase "I pity the fool!" In 1985 he teamed with [[Hulk Hogan]] against [[Roddy Piper]] at WrestleMania.

Soviet-born Russian cellist and conductor, noted for inspiring and commissioning new works. He premiered more than 100 pieces and formed long-standing artistic partnerships with composers including [[Dmitri Shostakovich]], [[Sergei Prokofiev]], [[Leonard Bernstein]] and [[Benjamin Britten]]. Born in [[Baku]], he studied under his father and later at the Moscow Conservatory, and he began performing internationally in the 1940s. Recognized as a staunch advocate of [[Human rights|human rights]], he received the 1974 Award of the International League of Human Rights. In 1974 he and his wife, the soprano Galina Vishnevskaya, were stripped of Soviet citizenship and went into exile. He served as music director of the National Symphony Orchestra in Washington, D.C., from 1977 to 1994, and his citizenship was restored in 1990.

First caliph of the [[Umayyad Caliphate|Umayyad dynasty]] (r. 661–680). He was a relatively late follower of the Islamic prophet [[Muhammad]], opposing him until Muhammad captured Mecca in 630, after which he became one of Muhammad's scribes. Appointed by Caliph [[Abu Bakr]] as a deputy commander in the conquest of Syria, he rose under [[Umar]] and became governor of Syria under [[Uthman]]. He directed the war against the [[Byzantine Empire]], including the first Muslim naval campaigns. After Uthman's assassination in 656, he opposed the election of [[Ali]], and their armies fought to a stalemate at the Battle of Siffin in 657. He made [[Damascus]] his capital and designated his son Yazid as successor, instituting hereditary rule.

Libyan military officer and revolutionary who led [[Libya]] from 1969 to 2011. He came to power in a bloodless military coup in 1969 that deposed King Idris I, and became Revolutionary Chairman of the Libyan Arab Republic. He later served as Secretary General of the General People's Congress and, from 1979, as Brotherly Leader. Initially committed to Arab nationalism and Arab socialism, he later ruled according to his own political theory, outlined in *The Green Book*. He introduced [[Sharia]] and used oil revenues to expand health care and education. His foreign policy supported revolutionary movements and was linked to the 1988 bombing of [[Pan Am Flight 103]], which led to international sanctions. In 2003 he renounced weapons of mass destruction programs. Overthrown during the 2011 civil war, which was sparked by [[Arab Spring|Arab Spring]] protests, he was captured by rebel forces and killed under disputed circumstances.

Thai martial art and full-contact combat sport, also called Thai boxing or the Art of Eight Limbs. It combines stand-up striking with fists, elbows, knees and shins, along with sweeps and clinching techniques. Muay Thai evolved from earlier systems such as Muay Boran during the [[Ayutthaya Kingdom]], where it served military purposes. In the early 20th century, under King Rama VII, formal rules introduced gloves, padded shorts and timed rounds, and bouts were held at [[Bangkok]]'s Lumpinee and Rajadamnern Stadiums. Today it is the national sport of [[Thailand]], and fights are preceded by the Wai Kru dance honoring teachers. The sport spread internationally, where practitioners began competing in [[Kickboxing|kickboxing]] and mixed-rules matches. The professional league is governed by the Professional Boxing Association of Thailand.

[[Comedy]] by [[William Shakespeare]], thought to have been written in 1598 and 1599. Set in Messina, the play centers on two romantic pairings that emerge when a group of soldiers arrives in town. Claudio and Hero's [[Courtship|courtship]] is nearly ruined by the accusations of the villain Don John. The witty banter of Benedick and Beatrice supplies much of the humor. Through "noting," which sounds like "nothing" and means gossip, Benedick and Beatrice are tricked into confessing their love for each other. The play was included in the First Folio, published in 1623.

[[Amphibian|Amphibious]] goby fish of the subfamily Oxudercinae, able to survive long periods out of water. Mudskippers can grow up to 30 cm (12 in) long, and most are brownish green. Their eyes protrude from the top of a flat head, and their jointed pectoral fins work like limbs, allowing them to crawl, climb low branches and "skip" across mud. They can leap up to 61 centimeters (24 in) by flexing and pushing with their tails. Males develop bright spots during mating seasons to attract females. They live on intertidal mudflats and in [[Mangrove|mangrove]] habitats.

Sudanese religious and political leader who claimed to be the Mahdi, the redeemer prophesied in [[Islam]]. In 1881 he launched a war against Egyptian rule in [[Sudan]], culminating in a victory at the Siege of [[Khartoum]]. He created a vast Islamic state extending from the [[Red Sea]] to [[Central Africa]], and his movement remained influential in Sudan a century later. The Mahdist State, whose supporters were called the Ansar, was dissolved after the Anglo-Egyptian conquest of Sudan in 1899. After his death from typhus, his chief deputy, Abdallahi ibn Muhammad, took over the administration. In the late 20th century his descendant Sadiq al-Mahdi twice served as prime minister of Sudan (1966–1967 and 1986–1989).
